tagline.text: Home of Cebu's second-highest peak, Mt. Kapayas, and its caves

location.label: Location
location.text: Catmon, northeastern Cebu Island (about 57 km north of Cebu City)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,000–2,500 (per person, day hike, transport and guide included)

children.text: Catmon is a municipality about 57 km north of Cebu City, famous for the trail up Mt. Kapayas (Torre Peak), the second-highest peak in Cebu. Its appeal is a challenging one-day hike over steep mossy-forest ridges to a 360-degree view and on to Lumanoy Cave.
Catmon lies about
57 km

north of Cebu City, with a northeastern coastal strip on the Camotes Sea and mountains inland. It covers about 110 km² and has 20 barangays and roughly 34,600 residents (2024 census). The municipal hall stands on the Cebu North Road. Between town and the village at the trailhead there is an unpaved road, so allow plenty of travel time if you plan to hike.

Catmon was founded by Spanish settlers in 1835. In 1903, at the request of the American authorities, it was merged with neighboring Sogod to form one municipality, and Sogod split off again in 1921. The name comes from the katmon trees that grew here. The patron saint is St. William the Hermit; the town fiesta is held every February 10, along with the Budbod Kabog festival, in which public schools take part.

For travelers, the main reason to come to Catmon is Mt. Kapayas. Also called Torre Peak, it stands in Sitio Kampanya, Barangay Kabangkaya (also spelled Cambangkaya), and is known as the second-highest peak in Cebu. Its height is given as about 766–783 m depending on the source, and it is classified as a Key Biodiversity Area. From the summit a 360-degree view opens over Catmon, nearby cities and toward Carmen, Tuburan and Danao. The forest and ridges around the summit offer chances to watch wild plants and birds, so do not pick plants or leave trash in the forest.

The mountain was closed for a time after earthquake and typhoon damage and was announced to reopen to trekkers from January 2026. Before climbing you must register at the Catmon municipal hall, attend a safety orientation at the municipal social hall and sign a waiver. There is also an announcement that climbs postponed by the earthquake get priority. Facilities and rules can change, so be sure to check the latest announcements. Catmon is not a beach resort but a destination centered on the mountain and the local community. It has no large facilities, but that makes it quiet and lets you feel local hospitality up close. Combine your hike with the falls in neighboring Sogod or the coast at Danao and you can tour northeastern Cebu fully. If your time is short, the Mt. Kapayas day hike alone is satisfying enough.

The second-highest mountain in Cebu, a challenging course through mossy forest, steep slopes and sharp limestone sections. According to trip reports, one group took about three hours from Cambangkaya to the summit, and with transport included it takes a full day. Some limestone sections near the top require using your hands, so gloves help. If you are not confident in your fitness, talk to your guide and allow generous rest intervals.

From the summit you look down on Catmon and neighboring cities, the mountain ranges toward Carmen, Tuburan and Danao, and the northern Cebu coastline. Clear mornings give the best visibility. Clouds block the view, so it is best to pick a day with good weather, and it is safer not to linger on top but to head down early.

A cave reached by a path that branches off the Torre Peak trail. The entrance is narrow and the steps are slippery, so a headlamp is needed. Formal exploration records are scarce, but it is said to be open to the public as part of the trek.

The Catmon local guides' association helps with registration and guiding. Hiking with local residents is safer and helps local incomes. Guides know the trail and weather changes well and are a big help on a first visit.
A beach is reported in Barangay Panalipan. It is a good place to rest after a hike, but facilities may be basic, so bring your own water and snacks.
The town fiesta is held on February 10 for St. William's feast day, together with the Budbod Kabog festival. The town gets crowded at this time, so find lodging early.

Driving along the Cebu North Road, coast and mountain scenery alternate. It is a good drive leading on to Sogod and Danao. In the roadside villages the buses pass through, you can also find small shops selling snacks.
In foothill villages such as Agsuwao, farming and daily life go on. Stop by before or after your hike to taste local snacks.
Take a Ceres bus from the North Bus Terminal in Cebu City to Catmon town.
In town, register at the municipal hall and complete the safety orientation and waiver signing. This process can take time, so it is best to arrive early.
Take a habal-habal to Sitio Kampanya (the trailhead). If you go by car, Agsuwao is the last point four-wheeled vehicles can reach.
Start the climb with your guide. Bring plenty of water (about 3 liters).
Enjoy the summit view and have lunch.
Head down. The steep sections are slippery, so descend slowly.
Return to town and catch the bus back.
A one-day schedule is tight, so if possible stay the night before in town or near Cebu City and start early. After the descent, warm up with a hot meal at a town restaurant.
At the trailhead, decide the route with your guide.
Take the path branching off Torre Peak to Lumanoy Cave.
Look around the cave carefully with a headlamp.
Return and begin the descent.
Return to town, report your descent in the registration book and thank your guide with a tip.
Do not enter the cave without a guide.
From Manila (NAIA) to Mactan-Cebu International Airport (CEB), the direct flight takes about
1 hour 30 minutes
From the airport, travel north through Cebu City for about
57 km
Take a Ceres bus bound for Catmon from the North Bus Terminal and get off in the town proper (Catmon Proper).
A short walk from town brings you to the habal-habal stand, which takes you to Sitio Kampanya.
Travel time and fares vary with traffic, so check at the terminal.
Enter the Catmon municipal hall in your navigation app and ask for directions toward Agsuwao. This is the last point four-wheeled vehicles can reach.
After that it is habal-habal or on foot. The road is rough and may be too much for an ordinary vehicle.
If you leave your car and climb, ask a villager about parking and do not leave valuables in the car.
Groups can arrange a van, multicab or truck through the local guides.
The dry season from December to May is best for climbing. The mossy forest and limestone sections are less slippery and the views are clear.
In the rainy and typhoon seasons there is a risk of landslides and rockfall, and climbing may be restricted. Check with the municipal office before you leave whether climbing is allowed.
It can be windier and cooler on the mountain than below, so bring a thin windproof layer. Starting before sunrise lets you avoid the midday heat.

Catmon town does not have many large hotels, so you can check small lodgings in a map app or stay near Cebu City and start early. Many travelers also use a beach lodging in Sogod or Danao as their base.

Filipino home cooking at town restaurants is the basic. Prepare a simple breakfast and packed lunch before the hike. There are no shops at the summit, so water and energy snacks are essential. For a hiking lunch, rice balls, bread and bananas that do not spoil easily are good.
There are almost no restaurants in the mountain villages, so buy everything you need in town before going up.

To recover after a hike, you can move to a beach lodging in Sogod or Danao to rest. Conversely, many people stay in town the day before for a dawn climb. In high season and on holidays lodging fills early, so book ahead.
Check the climbing permit status and schedule with the municipal office before you leave. Rules may change in the early period after the 2026 reopening.
Permit and guide fees are reported differently by different sources, so confirm them with the municipal office.
Plan your day so that you come down from the summit before sunset.
Bring about 3 liters of water, a headlamp, gloves and a change of clothes.
The limestone sections are sharp, so wear sturdy hiking boots and gloves.
Enter the cave only with a guide.
Agree on the habal-habal fare as a round trip before you go up.
Check beforehand how far your hiking or travel insurance coverage extends.
Sleep early the night before the hike and hydrate well.
Mt. Kapayas has steep slopes, mossy rock and sharp limestone, and is difficult for beginners. Always climb with a local guide.
In the rainy season there is a risk of landslides and rockfall.
Mobile signal is weak, so download offline maps.
The inside of the cave is dark and slippery.
Climbing rules and whether the mountain is open may change after earthquake and typhoon damage.
Do not leave your guide's side, so you do not get lost on the mountain.
If it rains on the mountain, descend immediately. There is a risk of rockfall and flash water.
